One more end-user wording case for this card, measured during the SCIM run for objectstack-ai/cloud#3667 (pin `e24136c2`).

An employee whose identity provider deactivated them through SCIM (`active:false`) and who then tries the password sign-in sees:

> You have been banned from this application. Please contact support if you believe this is an error.

The ban carries the reason `Deactivated via SCIM`. For that case the page should say something like "Your account has been deactivated by your organization. Contact your administrator." "Banned" reads as a disciplinary action, and "contact support" points them at the vendor rather than their own IT. The same applies to the refusal the API returns (`BANNED_USER`) when the ban reason is the SCIM one.

The maintainer answered both decision cards of 6845651657 in the seat thread (2026-11-13 22:19Z).

**Item 4 → A: a per-provider "sign out of the company sign-in too" switch, off by default.**
- Each SSO provider gets its own switch; nothing changes until an administrator turns it on.
- With it on, signing out of the platform also ends the company sign-in session, for SAML and OIDC alike.
- SAML: the provider stores its identity provider's logout address, and logout messages coming back from the identity provider are accepted only when signed.
- Saving the switch on a provider that cannot honour it (an OIDC provider with no logout endpoint, a SAML provider with no logout address) is refused loudly.
- Work: a server card (switch, SAML and OIDC wiring, signature requirement, logout address field, spec description) and a ui card (form item, sign-out redirect).

**Item 5 → D: honour the existing SSO-only switch.**
- When an environment has SSO-only mode on, the server refuses to give an IdP-provisioned user a local password at every door. The one exception is a managed platform administrator setting their own break-glass password, the same exception the cloud-hosted rule already has.
- When SSO-only mode is off, behaviour is unchanged, and the administrator's set-password action warns that it gives a managed user a way to sign in that bypasses the company sign-in.
- Not retroactive: managed users who already hold a local password are a separate question.
- Work: a server card (the refusal, the exception, pins, the `ssoOnlyMode` description), a governed ADR-0135 D5.2 note (kept in step with cloud ADR-0024 D5.2), and a ui card (the warning).

2026-11-14T04:35Z **One more measured case: `EMAIL_DOMAIN_NOT_ALLOWED` still shows the generic "link expired" headline, on 18.4.0.**

**Where.** Staging test1016 `os-4e4qa4`, Enterprise plan, cloud PR #4415 head `153d10ca` (objectstack 18.4.0). The provider is a real Okta OIDC app (`okta`, domain `objectlab.ai` verified, JIT on).

**What happened.** An Okta user whose email is `qa.sub@dev.objectlab.ai` (a subdomain, so unlisted) used the login page's 「Sign in with SSO」.
- The server refused it correctly. The container logged `[sso] account creation refused: the address is not at a domain the provider has proven {"code":"EMAIL_DOMAIN_NOT_ALLOWED","providerId":"okta","method":"sso-oidc"}`, and no account was created.
- The callback lands on `/_console/login?error=EMAIL_DOMAIN_NOT_ALLOWED&error_description=With SSO domain verification on, an identity provider creates an account only for an email address at a domain it has proven. Nothing was created.`
- The banner reads **"Single sign-on could not be completed — the sign-in link expired or was already used. Please try again."** The real code appears only behind 「Technical details」.

**Why.** `ui/apps/console/src/pages/auth/ssoCallbackRefusal.ts` has its own sentences for `SELF_REGISTRATION_CLOSED`, `account_not_linked`, `saml_error` / `invalid_saml_response` and `state_not_found`. Every other code falls back to `oauthCallbackFailed`. `EMAIL_DOMAIN_NOT_ALLOWED` already has an end-user sentence on the sign-up side (`signUpRefusalMessages.ts:65`, `auth.register.errors.emailDomainNotAllowed`), but the SSO callback mapping does not use it.

**Impact.** "Please try again" sends the person into a loop that can never succeed. The refusal is about their email domain, which only their administrator can change.

**Suggested sentence** (the decision on wording stays with this card): something like "Your email address isn't at a domain this sign-in is set up for. Ask your administrator."
